newsitem.title: FRANCE: Big Algerian vote reported for draft constitution.
newsitem.headline: Big Algerian vote reported for draft constitution.

text.p: Algerians have voted overwhelmingly in favour of a draft constitution that would ban Islamic political parties, Algeria's state radio reported on Friday.
The radio, basing its report on provisional referendum returns from several regions, said there would be a large "yes" vote. Official results were expected later on Friday.

State media said threats of violence by Moslem militants did not materialise. Official figures showed Algerians had turned out in large numbers to vote in defiance of the threats and calls by main opposition leaders for a boycott.
Polls closed at 8 p.m. (1900) on Thursday, but by early evening nearly three-quarters of Algeria's 16.4 million eligible voters had cast ballots, state radio said, quoting the Interior Ministry.

Residents in the garrison town of Blida, 50 km (30 miles) south of Algiers, said the army shelled mountains near the city on Wednesday night, apparently trying to pre-empt any buildup of Moslem guerrillas. Blida is a route for Moslem guerrillas seeking to carry out attacks around Algiers.
The planned constitution would ban Moslem militants from gaining power and guerrillas threatened before the referendum that they would kill anyone voting.
The national turnout was 71.94 percent at about 6 p.m (1700 GMT), compared to 65.82 percent in last year's presidential election at the same time, official figures showed.
President Liamine Zeroual's government hoped for a large turnout to bolster its popularity.
However, Algerian radio said turnout was only about 22 percent in two northeastern Berber provinces where a Berber-dominated party had called for a boycott.
The draft constitution, which says Arabic is the sole state language, angered Berber activists who want official recognition for their language as well.
Residents said they saw many "Yes" ballots thrown away near polling stations in Algiers, apparently by voters opposed to the proposed constitution.
Algiers-based diplomats said the government deployed more than 300,000 soldiers and policemen to guard voters across the country, five times the size of France.
Police and paramilitary forces were seen patrolling Algiers streets under drizzling rain and soldiers in combat gear manned roadblocks on main routes outside the city, witnesses said.
More than 60,000 people have died in Algeria's violence since 1992 when the authorities annulled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a huge lead.
The Armed Islamic Group, or GIA -- most feared of the country's Moslem guerrilla movements -- warned people not to vote on Thursday, threatening to slit the throats of anyone who left home.
A smiling Zeroual, who cast his ballot at a polling station near the presidential palace in Algiers, vowed to respect the voters' decision on his proposed reforms.
"The Algerian people is sovereign. Its will would be respected," Zeroual, a former army general, told reporters after he voted amid tight security.
Diplomats said hopes for change flowered last year but withered when violence continued and people felt the hardship of economic reforms required by overseas creditors.
"A year after the presidential election, political deadlock is still total," secular opposition leader Said Saadi said on Wednesday. "Social poverty is worsening every day."

"Even before the results of the referendum are known, the conclusions on the future of democracy are far from being optimistic," the Algerian Liberte newspaper said in a comment blasting the government for its tight control on the media.
